content:
Your Permit Came Back Rejected. Now What?

Getting a building permit rejected in Houston is frustrating, but it is also normal. Most commercial projects and many residential ones receive at least one round of plan review comments before approval. A rejection is not a "no". It is a list of things the reviewer needs fixed or explained before the permit can be issued.

What matters is how fast and how completely you respond. A clear, well-organized resubmittal can get you approved on the next round. A rushed or partial response usually leads to a second rejection and weeks of extra delay. This guide walks through exactly what to do, step by step.

Step 1: Read Every Comment Before Changing Anything

Download the full set of review comments and read all of them first, from every discipline. Houston plan review can involve several reviewers, such as building, structural, energy, fire, and site or drainage, and their comments often affect each other. A change that answers the structural reviewer can create a new issue for the energy or fire reviewer if you fix things one at a time.

Make a simple list with one line per comment: the reviewer, the sheet it applies to, what is being asked, and who on your team will fix it.

Step 2: Sort Comments Into Three Groups

  • Missing information: a detail, note, schedule, or calculation the reviewer could not find. These are usually quick fixes.
  • Code compliance issues: something in the design does not meet the adopted code, such as egress width, fire separation, energy requirements, or accessibility. These need a real design change.
  • Engineering issues: missing or insufficient structural calculations, foundation design, wind load analysis, or MEP sizing. These need a licensed engineer, and in most cases a PE stamp on the revised drawings.

Sorting this way tells you how big the job really is and who needs to be involved.

Step 3: Know the Houston-Specific Issues

Houston is different from most large U.S. cities in a few ways that show up in plan review comments:

  • No traditional zoning, but real rules: Houston does not have citywide zoning, but development is still controlled by city development ordinances, including building lines and setbacks, platting requirements, and private deed restrictions. Comments about building lines or plats are common on new construction.
  • Drainage and floodplain: Many Houston sites are in or near a floodplain. Expect comments on finished floor elevations, detention, and drainage if your site is affected.
  • Expansive clay soils: Houston's clay soils shrink and swell. Reviewers look closely at foundation design, so slab and pier designs often need engineering backed by soil information.
  • Wind loads: Houston is close to the Gulf Coast, so wind design and connection details are reviewed carefully, especially for roofs, canopies, and signage.

Step 4: Revise the Drawings, Not Just the Words

A common mistake is writing a response letter that says "noted" or "will comply" without actually changing the drawings. Reviewers check the sheets, not your promises. Every comment should point to a specific revision: a new detail, an updated note, a revised calculation, or a clarified dimension.

Cloud each change on the drawings and use a revision number and date in the title block, so the reviewer can find your fixes quickly.

Step 5: Write a Clear Comment Response Letter

Your response letter is what the reviewer reads first. Keep it simple:

  1. Copy each comment exactly as written.
  2. Write a short, direct response under it.
  3. Give the exact sheet and detail number where the fix is shown.

For example: "Comment 4: Provide foundation design for new addition. Response: Foundation plan and details added on sheet S-101, details 3 and 4. Structural calculations included in the resubmittal package." A reviewer can check that in a minute.

Step 6: Get Engineering Comments Stamped

If comments involve structural, foundation, or MEP design, the revised drawings and calculations usually must be sealed by a licensed Professional Engineer. Resubmitting unstamped engineering changes is one of the fastest ways to get rejected again. If your original designer is not available or not licensed in Texas, a licensed engineering firm can review the comments, redesign what is needed, and stamp the corrected sheets.

Step 7: Resubmit Complete, Not Piece by Piece

Resubmit everything at once: revised drawings, calculations, the response letter, and any required forms. Partial resubmittals often restart the clock and create confusion about which version is current. Double-check that every sheet in the set carries the same revision number before you upload.

How to Avoid the Next Rejection

  • Coordinate architectural, structural, and MEP drawings before submitting, so sheets do not contradict each other.
  • Include structural calculations and soil information with the first submittal, not after a comment asks for them.
  • Check site issues early: building lines, plat status, floodplain, and drainage.
  • Use a pre-submittal review by an experienced engineer to catch the usual problems.

faq.question: What should I do first when my Houston permit is rejected?
faq.answer: Download and read every plan review comment from all disciplines before changing anything, then list each comment with the sheet it affects and who will fix it.

faq.question: Do revised structural drawings need a PE stamp?
faq.answer: In most cases yes. Structural, foundation, and MEP revisions and calculations generally must be sealed by a licensed Professional Engineer before resubmittal.

faq.question: Does Houston have zoning?
faq.answer: Houston has no citywide zoning, but building lines, setbacks, platting rules, and private deed restrictions still apply and often appear in plan review comments.

faq.question: How can I avoid a second rejection?
faq.answer: Revise the actual drawings for every comment, write a clear response letter with sheet references, include stamped calculations where needed, and resubmit the complete package at once.
